items.stem: A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in many AWS accounts. The accounts belong to one organization in AWS Organizations. The security team works from one dedicated security account and wants to manage the solution for all member accounts from there. The security team must receive an alert when an instance communicates with IP addresses that are known to be malicious. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: communicates with IP addresses that are known to be malicious

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.
options.why: GuardDuty compares activity with [lists of malicious IP addresses and domains](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-uses-threat-intel-and-ml), and its administrator can [manage GuardDuty for all the member accounts](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-delegated-admin-organizations).

options.text: Activate Amazon Inspector for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.
options.why: Inspector scans workloads for [software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-dg-vulnerabilities-exposure), not for traffic to known malicious IP addresses.

options.text: Enable Amazon Detective for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.
options.why: Detective [simplifies the process of investigating security findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-vs-guardduty-vs-security-hub); the service that watches for malicious activity is GuardDuty.

options.text: Install an open-source security agent on every instance, send its output to an Amazon S3 bucket, and review the results in the security account.
options.why: It can work, but the team installs and updates agents on every instance; GuardDuty instead [pulls independent data streams directly](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-faq-no-need-to-enable-source-logs).
options.misconception: believes that a self-managed agent on every instance is as little work as a managed detection service

items.explanation: Traffic to a known malicious IP address is activity, and activity is what GuardDuty watches. GuardDuty uses [threat intelligence feeds](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-uses-threat-intel-and-ml) to spot it. [The delegated GuardDuty administrator account](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-delegated-admin-organizations) manages the member accounts, and [you don't need to enable anything else](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-foundational-nothing-else-to-enable) for the foundational data sources.
items.takeaway: Traffic to a known malicious IP address is activity: GuardDuty. A vulnerable package is software: Inspector.
items.twin: If the stem said "runs a software package that has a published common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVE) entry" instead: Amazon Inspector, because it scans for [software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-dg-vulnerabilities-exposure).
items.say: Traffic to a known bad IP address is activity, so I'd enable GuardDuty for the whole organization.

solvers.stem_only: Amazon GuardDuty enabled organization-wide through a delegated administrator in the security account; its threat intelligence produces findings for EC2 traffic to known malicious IPs.

items.stem: A company stores call transcripts as text objects in many Amazon S3 buckets across several AWS accounts. Some transcripts contain sensitive data such as credit card numbers. Auditors require the company to identify which objects contain credit card numbers. The check must run again every day so that it also covers the transcripts that arrive after the first check. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: identify which objects contain credit card numbers

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty S3 Protection in the accounts, and review the findings that it generates for the buckets that hold the transcripts.
options.why: S3 Protection monitors [AWS CloudTrail data events for Amazon S3](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-s3-protection-data-events) to find threats such as data exfiltration, not card numbers inside objects.

options.text: Write an AWS Lambda function that runs a regular expression for card numbers on every object each day, and store the matches in a table.
options.why: It can work, but the team writes and maintains the code; Macie managed data identifiers already detect [credit card numbers and bank account numbers](../facts/macie.md#macie-managed-data-identifiers).
options.misconception: believes that a custom scanner is as little work to run as a managed detection service

options.text: Create an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job for the buckets that runs daily and uses the managed data identifiers for card numbers.
options.why: Macie managed data identifiers detect [credit card numbers and bank account numbers](../facts/macie.md#macie-managed-data-identifiers), and a job can run [on a recurring basis for periodic analysis](../facts/macie.md#macie-discovery-jobs-targeted).

options.text: Create an AWS Config rule that checks that default encryption is turned on for every bucket, and review the buckets that are noncompliant.
options.why: A Config rule [represents desired configurations for a resource](../facts/config.md#config-faq-rule-desired-configuration), such as bucket encryption; a bucket setting does not show which objects hold card numbers.
options.misconception: believes that the encryption settings of a bucket show what data its objects hold

items.explanation: Card numbers inside objects are sensitive data in Amazon S3, and Macie [discovers sensitive data by using machine learning](../facts/macie.md#macie-dg-discovers-sensitive-data) and pattern matching. A sensitive data discovery job gives [deeper, more targeted analysis](../facts/macie.md#macie-discovery-jobs-targeted) of the buckets that you choose, and a job that runs [on a recurring basis for periodic analysis](../facts/macie.md#macie-discovery-jobs-targeted), such as daily, covers new transcripts without code.
items.takeaway: Card numbers or PII inside S3 objects point to Macie; threats against S3 point to GuardDuty.
items.twin: If the stem said "scan each new transcript for malware when it is uploaded" instead: GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3, because [GuardDuty automatically starts a malware scan](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-malware-s3-scans-new-uploads) on each upload.
items.say: Card numbers inside S3 objects are sensitive data, so I'd run a scheduled Macie discovery job.

solvers.stem_only: Amazon Macie with a scheduled (daily) sensitive data discovery job, using managed data identifiers for credit card numbers, managed from a Macie administrator account.

items.stem: A company runs a payment application on AWS. As part of an annual audit, an external auditor asks the company for the AWS SOC 2 report and the AWS PCI DSS attestation of compliance. The auditor will use these documents to assess the controls of the AWS data centers and services that the application uses. The auditor reviews the company's own controls separately. What should a solutions architect do to provide these documents?
keywords: assess the controls of the AWS data centers and services

options.text: Enable the PCI DSS standard in AWS Security Hub CSPM, and export the control findings for the auditor.
options.why: CSPM controls check the company's own resources, and its standards [don't guarantee compliance with any regulatory frameworks](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-no-compliance-guarantee); they are not AWS reports.

options.text: Download the documents from AWS Artifact in the AWS Management Console, and send them to the auditor.
options.why: AWS Artifact gives [on-demand downloads of AWS security and compliance documents](../facts/artifact.md#artifact-guide-on-demand-compliance-documents), such as SOC and PCI reports about AWS itself.

options.text: Deploy an AWS Config conformance pack for PCI DSS in every account, and send the compliance results to the auditor.
options.why: A conformance pack holds [AWS Config rules and remediation actions](../facts/config.md#config-guide-conformance-pack) that check the company's own resources, not the AWS data centers.

options.text: Run Amazon Inspector CIS scans on all Amazon EC2 instances, and send the scan reports to the auditor.
options.why: CIS scans [benchmark your Amazon EC2 instance operating systems](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-cis-scans), which belong to the company, so the result is not an AWS audit report.
options.misconception: believes that a benchmark scan of the company's instances is an AWS audit report

items.explanation: The auditor asks for reports that AWS writes about the AWS side. AWS Artifact gives [on-demand downloads of AWS security and compliance documents](../facts/artifact.md#artifact-guide-on-demand-compliance-documents), such as [System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports](../facts/artifact.md#artifact-guide-on-demand-compliance-documents). These documents show [the security and compliance of the AWS infrastructure](../facts/artifact.md#artifact-guide-audit-artifacts-for-auditors); the company proves its own controls with its own evidence.
items.takeaway: AWS SOC and PCI reports about AWS itself come from AWS Artifact, not from checks of your resources.
items.twin: If the stem said "evidence that the company's own resources follow PCI DSS" instead: the PCI DSS standard in Security Hub CSPM, because a standard is [a set of requirements](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-standard-definition) checked against the company's resources.
items.say: AWS's own SOC and PCI reports come from AWS Artifact; my checks only cover my side.

solvers.stem_only: Download the AWS SOC 2 report and PCI DSS AOC from AWS Artifact (self-service portal for AWS compliance reports) and give them to the auditor.

items.stem: A company has recorded the configuration of its resources with AWS Config in all its accounts and Regions for the past year. During an audit, an auditor asks which inbound rules one specific security group had at a point in time three months ago. Engineers have changed the security group several times since then. Which AWS service or feature should a solutions architect use to answer the auditor's question?
keywords: inbound rules one specific security group had at a point in time
recorded the configuration of its resources

options.text: Review the AWS CloudTrail event history for the security group to see its inbound rules on that date.
options.why: CloudTrail answers [who made an API call](../facts/config.md#config-faq-vs-cloudtrail) that changed the group; the auditor asks what the group looked like on one date.

options.text: Review the Amazon GuardDuty findings of the account to see the inbound rules of the security group on that date.
options.why: GuardDuty [continuously monitors your AWS accounts, workloads, runtime activity](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-dg-continuous-malicious-activity) for malicious activity; its findings are not a history of security group rules.

options.text: Review the AWS Security Hub CSPM security score of the account to see the inbound rules of the security group on that date.
options.why: CSPM uses the results of its checks [to calculate security scores](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-security-score); a score is a summary, not a record of past rules.
options.misconception: believes that a security score stores the past configuration of each resource

options.text: Review the configuration history of the security group in AWS Config to see its configuration item for that date.
options.why: A configuration item is [a point-in-time view of the various attributes](../facts/config.md#config-guide-configuration-item) of a resource, so the history shows the group as it was.

items.explanation: The auditor asks what the security group looked like, not who changed it. AWS Config keeps a [resource inventory, configuration history, and configuration change notifications](../facts/config.md#config-faq-what-it-is). Because Config was recording, its history shows [the port rules that were open](../facts/config.md#config-guide-security-analysis-history) on the date that the auditor names.
items.takeaway: What a resource looked like at a past time: AWS Config. Who changed it: AWS CloudTrail.
items.twin: If the stem said "which engineer changed the inbound rules" instead: AWS CloudTrail, because it [records user API activity on your account](../facts/config.md#config-faq-cloudtrail-records-api-activity) with the identity of the caller.
items.say: What the group looked like then is a Config question; who changed it is a CloudTrail question.

solvers.stem_only: AWS Config configuration history (configuration items / resource timeline) for the security group at that point in time.

citations: www/cloudtrail/faqs#You can visit the AWS CloudTrail console

items.stem: A company uses AWS Organizations. Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector, and Amazon Macie already run in every member account in two AWS Regions, each with a delegated administrator in a security account. The security team wants to centrally manage the findings of all three services as one prioritized list, in one Region, from the security account. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: centrally manage the findings of all three services
one prioritized list, in one Region

options.text: Enable Amazon Detective in the security account, add the member accounts to its behavior graph, and use Detective as the list of findings.
options.why: Detective [simplifies the process of investigating security findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-vs-guardduty-vs-security-hub); the service that [aggregates, organizes, and prioritizes your security alerts](../facts/detective.md#detective-vs-guardduty-vs-security-hub) is Security Hub.

options.text: Enable AWS Security Hub for the organization with the security account as delegated administrator, and turn on cross-Region aggregation to one home Region.
options.why: Security Hub [also receives findings from other AWS services](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-receives-service-findings) such as GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie, and aggregation brings them [to a single home Region](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-cross-region-aggregation).

options.text: Create Amazon EventBridge rules in every account and Region that invoke an AWS Lambda function to write each finding to a dashboard database.
options.why: It can work, but the team builds and runs rules, code and a database in every account and Region; Security Hub integrations [are activated automatically](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-integrations-auto-activated).
options.misconception: believes that a home-built findings pipeline is less work than a managed aggregator

options.text: Create an AWS Config aggregator for the organization in the security account, and use it to view the findings of the three services.
options.why: An aggregator collects [configuration and compliance data from multiple source accounts](../facts/config.md#config-guide-aggregator-read-only), not the findings of GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie.

items.explanation: The services already detect problems; the team needs one place for their findings. Security Hub CSPM gives [a single pane of glass](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-receives-service-findings) for findings from GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie, and most integrations [are activated automatically](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-integrations-auto-activated). Macie is the exception to check: you configure it to [also send sensitive data findings](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-macie-policy-findings-default). Cross-Region aggregation brings findings, insights and scores [to a single home Region](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-cross-region-aggregation).
items.takeaway: One prioritized list of findings across accounts and Regions: Security Hub with a delegated administrator and a home Region.
items.twin: If the stem said "determine the root cause of one GuardDuty finding" instead: Amazon Detective, because it helps [identify the root cause of security findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-dg-root-cause).
items.say: Security Hub is the one queue for every finding, with one home Region for all Regions.

solvers.stem_only: AWS Security Hub enabled for the organization with the security account as delegated administrator, plus cross-Region aggregation into one home Region; it ingests GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie findings in one normalized list.

items.stem: A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in many AWS accounts. The accounts belong to one organization in AWS Organizations. The security team works from one dedicated security account and wants to manage the solution for all member accounts from there. The security team must receive an alert when an instance runs a software package that has a published common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVE) entry. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: runs a software package that has a published common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVE) entry

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.
options.why: GuardDuty [continuously monitors your AWS accounts, workloads, runtime activity](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-dg-continuous-malicious-activity) for malicious activity; a vulnerable package is a weakness in software, not activity.

options.text: Activate Amazon Inspector for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.
options.why: Inspector scans for [software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-dg-vulnerabilities-exposure) and rescans after [a new common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVE)](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-no-scheduled-assessments) entry affects a resource.

options.text: Enable Amazon Detective for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.
options.why: Detective helps [identify the root cause of security findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-dg-root-cause); scanning the packages of an instance for CVEs is the job of Inspector.

options.text: Install an open-source security agent on every instance, send its output to an Amazon S3 bucket, and review the results in the security account.
options.why: It can work, but the team installs and patches an agent on every instance; Amazon Inspector is activated [for your entire organization with a single click](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-delegated-admin-organizations).
options.misconception: believes that a self-managed scanner on every instance is as little work as a managed scanning service

items.explanation: A package with a published CVE is a weakness in software, and software is what Inspector scans. With Inspector you [don't need to manually schedule or configure](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-no-scheduled-assessments) assessment scans: it rescans after a new CVE is published. [The delegated administrator account for Amazon Inspector](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-delegated-admin-organizations) manages the whole organization from the security account.
items.takeaway: A vulnerable package is software: Inspector. Traffic to a known malicious IP address is activity: GuardDuty.
items.twin: If the stem said "communicates with IP addresses that are known to be malicious" instead: Amazon GuardDuty, because it uses [lists of malicious IP addresses and domains](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-uses-threat-intel-and-ml).
items.say: A package with a known CVE is a software weakness, so I'd activate Inspector for the organization.

solvers.stem_only: Amazon Inspector activated organization-wide through a delegated administrator; it scans EC2 instances (agentless or SSM agent) for software CVEs and produces findings.

items.stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. Administrators in member accounts have full permissions in their own accounts. The company must ensure that no one in a member account, including the root user, can turn off S3 Block Public Access at the account level. The company must also find every S3 bucket that has server access logging turned off, including buckets that already have it off today, and must turn logging back on automatically. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: including buckets that already have it off today

options.text: Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies the action that changes the account-level S3 Block Public Access settings.
options.why: The SCP applies [including the member account's root user](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user), and member principals [cannot remove or change SCPs that are applied to that account](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-faq-member-principals-cannot-change-scps).

options.text: Create an AWS Config rule in proactive mode that blocks any change to the account-level S3 Block Public Access settings.
options.why: Proactive rules evaluate resources before deployment, but [proactive rules do not remediate resources](../facts/config.md#config-guide-proactive-vs-detective) or stop their deployment.

options.text: Write an AWS Lambda function that runs every hour, checks the logging setting of every bucket, and turns logging on where it is off.
options.why: It can work, but the team writes and runs code on a schedule; AWS Config offers [a set of managed automation documents](../facts/config.md#config-guide-remediation-ssm-automation) for remediation.
options.misconception: believes that a scheduled custom script is less work than a managed rule with remediation

options.text: Create an AWS Config rule that checks server access logging on each bucket, with automatic remediation through a Systems Manager Automation document.
options.why: The rule [flags the resource as noncompliant](../facts/config.md#config-guide-rules-flag-noncompliant), detective rules [evaluate resources that have already been deployed](../facts/config.md#config-guide-proactive-vs-detective), and [you can either choose manual or automatic remediation](../facts/config.md#config-guide-remediation-ssm-automation).

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty in every member account, and use an Amazon EventBridge rule to turn logging back on when a finding arrives.
options.why: GuardDuty analyzes events such as [AWS CloudTrail management events](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-foundational-sources-list), so it reports logging being turned off; it does not check buckets that already had logging off.

items.explanation: The stem has two needs. Prevention against administrators and the root user needs an SCP, because [AWS Config rules do not prevent the user](../facts/config.md#config-faq-rules-evaluate-after-change-not-prevent) from making a change. Detection and repair of a bucket setting is a Config rule with [AWS Systems Manager Automation documents](../facts/config.md#config-guide-remediation-ssm-automation) as automatic remediation.
items.takeaway: Stop a change for everyone in member accounts with an SCP; find and fix drift with a Config rule and remediation.
items.twin: If the stem said "alert the team when an administrator turns off S3 Block Public Access" instead: an AWS Config rule alone, because a rule [flags the resource as noncompliant](../facts/config.md#config-guide-rules-flag-noncompliant) after the change.
items.say: To stop it I'd use an SCP; to find and fix it I'd use a Config rule with remediation.

solvers.stem_only: Preventive control that binds member-account root users: an SCP at the organization root (or on the OUs holding the member accounts) that denies s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock. Detective plus corrective control for existing and future buckets: the AWS Config managed rule for S3 bucket server access logging, which evaluates all current buckets, with automatic remediation through the Systems Manager Automation runbook that turns bucket logging on. No custom Lambda code needed.

items.stem: A company has used Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub CSPM, and Amazon Detective in all its accounts for a year. GuardDuty reports that an IAM role made API calls that are unusual for the role. A security engineer must determine the root cause. The engineer needs to see which IP addresses the role used during the past weeks and which API calls the role made. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
keywords: which IP addresses the role used during the past weeks

options.text: Open the finding in AWS Security Hub CSPM, and create an insight that groups the related findings of the role.
options.why: Security Hub [aggregates, organizes, and prioritizes your security alerts](../facts/detective.md#detective-vs-guardduty-vs-security-hub); grouping findings does not trace the IP addresses and API calls behind one finding.

options.text: Query the AWS CloudTrail logs in Amazon S3 with Amazon Athena, and write queries that group the role's calls by source IP address.
options.why: It can work, but the engineer writes and tunes queries; with Detective you do not [develop, configure, or tune your own queries](../facts/detective.md#detective-no-queries-to-build).
options.misconception: believes that writing queries over raw logs is the least development effort

options.text: Pivot from the GuardDuty finding into Amazon Detective, and review the activity of the role in the behavior graph.
options.why: The behavior graph holds [CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow logs, and GuardDuty findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-core-sources), and you pivot from the finding [directly into the Detective console](../facts/detective.md#detective-pivot-from-guardduty-security-hub).

options.text: Create a GuardDuty suppression rule for the finding type, and review the archived findings of the role.
options.why: A suppression rule archives matching findings, and [GuardDuty still generates all findings](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-suppression-rule-still-generates); archiving explains nothing about the cause.
options.misconception: believes that suppressing a finding explains its cause

items.explanation: The finding exists; the engineer needs its cause. Detective helps [quickly identify the root cause of security findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-definition-root-cause) from collected log data. Its behavior graph uses [CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow logs, and GuardDuty findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-core-sources), so the IP addresses and API calls of the role are already there, and the engineer writes no queries.
items.takeaway: Root cause of one finding without writing queries: Amazon Detective.
items.twin: If the stem said "keep the findings from every account in one prioritized list" instead: AWS Security Hub, because it [aggregates, organizes, and prioritizes your security alerts](../facts/detective.md#detective-vs-guardduty-vs-security-hub).
items.say: To find why a finding happened, I'd pivot into Detective and read the behavior graph.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST development effort.

I mark the constraints: the finding already exists, the engineer needs its root cause, and the engineer must see the role's IP addresses and API calls over the past weeks. Detective has run for a year, so its data covers that time.
Before I look at the options, I predict Amazon Detective, because it investigates an existing finding, and its behavior graph already holds CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow Logs and GuardDuty findings.

I remove the suppression rule, because GuardDuty still generates the findings and archiving explains nothing. I remove the Security Hub insight, because it groups findings but does not trace the activity of one role.
Between Detective and the Athena queries the difference is the code; the stem says LEAST development effort, so I choose Detective, where I write no queries.
Check: Detective shows the IP addresses and API calls of the role over time, and I pivot to it from the finding. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Pivot from the GuardDuty finding into Amazon Detective and use the behavior graph / role profile to see the IP addresses and API calls of the role over time.

items.stem: A startup runs Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS account and one AWS Region. The account has no AWS CloudTrail trail and no VPC flow logs. The startup needs to detect compromised instances and the use of stolen credentials as soon as possible. The startup wants a fully managed service and has no security engineers to tune detection logic. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: no AWS CloudTrail trail and no VPC flow logs
compromised instances and the use of stolen credentials

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty in the Region, and review the findings that it generates from its foundational data sources.
options.why: GuardDuty [pulls independent data streams directly](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-faq-no-need-to-enable-source-logs) from CloudTrail, flow logs and DNS logs, so enabling it is the whole task.

options.text: Turn on VPC flow logs, DNS query logging, and a CloudTrail trail first, and then enable Amazon GuardDuty in the Region.
options.why: It works, but the extra steps add nothing for GuardDuty: [you don't need to create or configure](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-flow-logs-not-required) VPC flow logs for it.

options.text: Send VPC flow logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and create metric filters and alarms for traffic patterns that suggest a compromised instance.
options.why: The team writes and tunes every filter, and flow logs hold no API calls; GuardDuty brings [threat intelligence feeds](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-uses-threat-intel-and-ml) and machine learning models.
options.misconception: believes that a home-built log analysis is a managed threat detection service

options.text: Activate Amazon Inspector in the Region, and use its network reachability scans to find the instances that are compromised.
options.why: Inspector finds [network reachability issues](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-ec2-network-reachability) and vulnerable packages; these are weaknesses, not an instance or credential that is already in use by an attacker.

items.explanation: GuardDuty reads [AWS CloudTrail management events](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-foundational-sources-list), VPC flow logs and DNS logs through its own streams. [You don't need to enable anything else](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-foundational-nothing-else-to-enable) for these foundational sources, and GuardDuty [does not affect any of your existing](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-flow-logs-not-required) flow logs configuration. Its findings include instance compromise and account compromise.
items.takeaway: GuardDuty needs no trail or flow logs from you: enable it, and it reads its own streams.
items.twin: If the stem said "keep the network logs for one year for later analysis" instead: turn on VPC flow logs to Amazon S3, because [GuardDuty does not manage or retain your logs](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-does-not-retain-logs).
items.say: GuardDuty pulls its own copy of the logs, so I'd turn it on and nothing else.

solvers.stem_only: Enable Amazon GuardDuty; it reads CloudTrail management events, VPC flow logs and DNS logs from its own independent streams, so no trail or flow logs need to be set up first.

items.stem: A company uses Amazon GuardDuty in all accounts of its organization, with a delegated administrator in a security account. The company already stores logs in a central Amazon S3 bucket in a log archive account. A new regulation requires the company to retain every GuardDuty finding for 2 years and to make the findings available for an audit on request. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: retain every GuardDuty finding for 2 years

options.text: Increase the finding retention period in the GuardDuty settings of the delegated administrator account to 2 years for all member accounts.
options.why: GuardDuty retains a finding for [90 days](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-finding-retention-90-days) at most, and this quota cannot be increased.

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function in each member account that copies the new GuardDuty findings to an Amazon DynamoDB table every day.
options.why: It can work, but it adds code in every account; GuardDuty can [optionally export the generated findings](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-export-findings-to-s3) to S3 from the administrator account.
options.misconception: believes that copying findings with custom code is less work than the built-in export

options.text: Turn on the GuardDuty integration with AWS Security Hub CSPM, and keep the GuardDuty findings in Security Hub CSPM for 2 years.
options.why: Security Hub CSPM saves a finding for [90 days](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-finding-retention-90-days) after its most recent update, so it is not a 2-year store.

options.text: Configure the GuardDuty delegated administrator account to export findings to the central S3 bucket, and keep the exported objects for 2 years.
options.why: Findings can be [exported to a central S3 bucket in the Log Archive account](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-sra-export-findings-log-archive) from the administrator, and S3 keeps them as long as the company sets.

items.explanation: GuardDuty keeps findings for [90 days](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-finding-retention-90-days), so a 2-year rule needs a copy outside GuardDuty. You can [optionally export the generated findings](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-export-findings-to-s3) to an S3 bucket. In the AWS reference architecture, findings are [exported to a central S3 bucket in the Log Archive account](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-sra-export-findings-log-archive) to [retain the findings beyond 90 days](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-sra-export-findings-log-archive). [GuardDuty is a Regional service](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-faq-regional-service), and its findings stay in their Region, so the administrator sets the export in each Region where GuardDuty runs.
items.takeaway: Findings expire inside the service; a long retention rule needs an export to Amazon S3.
items.twin: If the stem said "Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery results" instead: configure a Macie results repository, because Macie keeps the results [for only 90 days](../facts/macie.md#macie-results-90-days-export-s3-kms) without one.
items.say: GuardDuty keeps findings ninety days, so I'd export them to the central S3 bucket.

solvers.stem_only: GuardDuty keeps findings for a fixed 90 days; configure findings export from the delegated administrator to an S3 bucket (KMS-encrypted) and apply a 2-year retention / lifecycle on that bucket.

items.stem: A company lets customers upload documents to an Amazon S3 bucket through a web application. The company must scan each newly uploaded object for malware before other systems process the object. The company must also find personally identifiable information (PII) in the objects that the bucket stores. The company prefers fully managed AWS services. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: scan each newly uploaded object for malware

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 on the upload bucket, and use the scan result to decide which objects to process.
options.why: [GuardDuty automatically starts a malware scan](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-malware-s3-scans-new-uploads) when an object is uploaded to the selected bucket, with no scanning engine to run.

options.text: Enable Amazon Macie for the account, and configure Macie to scan each newly uploaded object in the bucket for malware.
options.why: Macie [discovers sensitive data by using machine learning](../facts/macie.md#macie-dg-discovers-sensitive-data); malware in new uploads is the job of GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3.

options.text: Enable Amazon Detective for the account, and use its behavior graph to find malware and PII in the uploaded objects.
options.why: The behavior graph is built from [CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow logs, and GuardDuty findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-core-sources), not from the content of objects.

options.text: Enable Amazon Macie, and run a sensitive data discovery job on the bucket that uses managed data identifiers for PII.
options.why: Macie managed data identifiers detect [personally identifiable information (PII)](../facts/macie.md#macie-managed-data-identifiers) such as passport numbers in S3 objects.

options.text: Create an AWS Lambda function that runs an open-source antivirus engine on each upload, and update its virus definitions every day.
options.why: It can work, but the team packages, runs and updates the engine; Malware Protection for S3 scans [newly uploaded objects](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-malware-s3-scans-new-uploads-managed) as a managed feature.
options.misconception: believes that a self-built antivirus pipeline is less work than a managed malware scan

items.explanation: The stem has two needs. Malware in each new upload is a GuardDuty job: Malware Protection for S3 scans [newly uploaded objects](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-malware-s3-scans-new-uploads-managed) in the buckets that you select. PII in stored objects is a Macie job, because Macie is a [fully managed sensitive data discovery service](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-faq-vs-macie).
items.takeaway: Malware in new S3 uploads: GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3. Sensitive data in stored objects: Macie.
items.twin: If the stem said "detect unusual API calls that read many objects from the bucket" instead: GuardDuty S3 Protection, because it monitors [AWS CloudTrail data events for Amazon S3](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-s3-protection-data-events).
items.say: Malware in uploads is GuardDuty Malware Protection; PII in stored objects is Macie.

solvers.stem_only: GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 on the upload bucket (scans new objects, tags results) and Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery for PII.

items.stem: A company uses AWS Security Hub CSPM in us-east-1 and us-west-2 for all accounts of its organization. The company has not enabled the new AWS Security Hub. The AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard is enabled in both Regions. Control findings appear for resources in us-east-1, but none appear for resources in us-west-2. The company currently records resource configurations with AWS Config in us-east-1 only. Which solution will produce the missing control findings with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Control findings appear for resources in us-east-1, but none appear for resources in us-west-2

options.text: Configure cross-Region aggregation with us-east-1 as the home Region and us-west-2 as a linked Region, so that the checks start in us-west-2.
options.why: Aggregation brings findings that already exist [to a single home Region](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-cross-region-aggregation); it does not create control findings that AWS Config never evaluated.

options.text: Write AWS Lambda functions in us-west-2 that check each resource against the standard and import the results into Security Hub CSPM as findings.
options.why: It can work, but the team writes and maintains checks that the standard already has; CSPM runs them itself after AWS Config records the resources.
options.misconception: believes that custom check code is less work than turning on the AWS Config dependency

options.text: Enable AWS Config in us-west-2 for every account in the organization, and record the resources that the controls of the standard check.
options.why: Security Hub CSPM [uses service-linked rules from AWS Config](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-uses-config-rules) for most controls, so recording in us-west-2 lets those controls run there.

options.text: Enable Amazon Detective in us-west-2 for every account in the organization, and turn on its source package for Security Hub CSPM data.
options.why: Detective [simplifies the process of investigating security findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-vs-guardduty-vs-security-hub); it reads findings and creates no control findings for a standard.

items.explanation: The standard is enabled in us-west-2, but most of its checks run on AWS Config. Security Hub CSPM [uses service-linked rules from AWS Config](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-uses-config-rules) for most controls, and [you must enable AWS Config and record resources](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-uses-config-rules) to get those control findings. Turning on Config with resource recording in us-west-2 for every account lets the existing controls produce findings.
items.takeaway: Security Hub CSPM control findings need AWS Config recording in every Region and account where CSPM runs.
items.twin: If the stem said "control findings appear in both Regions, but the team must review them from us-east-1" instead: cross-Region aggregation, because it brings findings [to a single home Region](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-cross-region-aggregation).
items.say: CSPM checks run on AWS Config, so I'd turn on Config recording in us-west-2 for every account.

solvers.stem_only: Security Hub CSPM controls depend on AWS Config recording in each Region; enable AWS Config recording in us-west-2 for every account.
